alternative: Use the runtime's ownership: kotlin.io.use (Closeable/AutoCloseable) for deterministic release, java.lang.ref.Cleaner for resources a library owns, and the GC - including Kotlin/Native's tracing memory manager - for memory; only interop boundaries (JNI handle tables, Objective-C interop) deal in counts.
idiom_name: none on the JVM - GC owns lifetime; use {} and Cleaner at the resource edge
implementation_notes: Kotlin's targets have tracing collectors: the JVM, and Kotlin/Native's modern memory manager, which the documentation describes as similar to the JVM and Go (objects live in a shared heap and a tracing GC collects what is unreachable), so there is no object-owned count to program against. What replaces the classic structure: use, documented since Kotlin 1.0 as executing the block and then closing the resource whether or not an exception is thrown, and java.lang.ref.Cleaner for resources a library must release when their owner disappears. Immutable values (data-class copy, read-only collections) share without any count.
pitfalls: use closes only what is in scope: an object stored in a field, or returned out of the block, is not released when the block exits.
On Kotlin/Native the GC decides when an object dies; observing a 'last reference' in your code is not deterministic and no per-object count is exposed.
Hand-written atomic counters on the JVM must respect the memory model, and finalizer-like hooks (Cleaner) are non-deterministic by design - delegate to the platform instead of inventing a count.
